title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
gist: A Harvard study of 718 firms using Jellyfish data (about 300 million work events, 700,000 workers) finds AI agents raise lines of code 30% but resolved Jira issues only 12%, because code review and other downstream steps absorb the extra output; assistants barely change completed work.

themes.theme: Output gains from AI coding tools

insights.claim: AI coding assistants raise code output only slightly (12% lines of code, 9% commits, 5% pull requests), with only the effect on commits statistically significant.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Assistant-style tools show weak measurable output gains, tempering ROI claims.
insights.locator: AI assistants lead to small increases in code output

insights.claim: AI agents produce large, significant output increases of 30% in lines of code, 20% in commits and 23% in pull requests.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Agentic tools change output volume far more than assistants do.
insights.locator: AI agents lead to large and significant increases

insights.claim: Coding assistants did not increase the number of resolved Jira issues, while agents brought a 12% increase, far below the estimated 30% increase in lines of code.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Completed work, not code volume, is the metric that matters for engineering ROI.
insights.locator: Coding assistant were found not to increase the number of resolved issues

insights.claim: Engineers spend only 30-40% of their time writing code, so when AI speeds code writing, complementary steps like planning, review, testing and deployment become bottlenecks.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Speeding up one stage of the pipeline shifts constraints downstream (Amdahl-style limits).
insights.quote: engineers spend 30-40% of their time writing code; the remainder goes to these complementary tasks
insights.locator: We impute time usage from the Jellyfish data

insights.claim: With AI adoption, average PR time to review rose 49%, comments per PR rose 53%, and the share of PRs requiring changes doubled.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Review capacity is the binding constraint; watch review-time metrics when rolling out agents.
insights.locator: Specifically, they found that the average PR time to review increased by 49%

insights.claim: The share of workers performing code reviews rose 14% with no improvement from using AI to assist reviews, and the added PR effort was not explained by larger PRs.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: AI review tools have not yet offset the added review load.
insights.locator: Additionally, the share of workers performing code reviews increased by 14%

insights.claim: The study covers roughly 300 million work events from 700,000 workers across 700+ firms between January 2021 and March 2026, drawing on HR, version control, issue tracking, calendar and generative-AI tool data.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Large-sample telemetry gives more credibility than vendor self-reports.
insights.locator: The study was based on approximately 300 million work events

insights.claim: Reddit commenters argued every line of code is a potential liability, and that agents are untrustworthy actors who can cause damage without malice while pursuing a task.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: More generated code means more surface for defects and hallucination risk.
insights.quote: every line of code is a potential liability
insights.locator: Commenting on the findings, Reddit user Prime_1

insights.claim: A commenter suggested mean time to recovery could become an increasingly important metric for AI's impact, since engineers who understand less of the code they ship will face more frequent and complicated issues.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Track MTTR alongside throughput as AI-written code scales.
